problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/6c6b1de6d32b1dbc2161f7446902c971cc7c179f71cdc2ce199c0e688af6f554.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(-1,-1)$ and $B(-1,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(1-2x)\,i+2y\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free, and the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ can be parametrized as*

$$
r=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$
worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)=-2+2=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that 

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095686/assets/212435c94989d0553db86b8d39edae3a7905d41ef668bb33fa0a62bed99d5462.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

We have the parametrization

$$
r(t)=(-1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-2x=1-2(-1)=3, \\ Q(x,y) & =2y=2(2t-1)=4t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)=0, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3)\cdot (2)-(4t-2)\cdot (0)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot {[t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\cdot 1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=6.
$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field with simply connected domain D⊆R2, then the following are equivalent:

  • F is a source-free vector field.

  • ∇⋅F=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=0.

  • The flux ∮CF⋅nds along any closed curve C∈D is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves C1,C2∈D with the same start and endpoints, we have that ∫C1F⋅nds=∫C2F⋅nds.

  • There exists a stream function ψ(x,y) for F.

First, notice that

∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=∂∂x(1−2x)+∂∂y(2y)=−2+2=0,

which shows that F is a source-free vector field.

Since F is source-free, we know the flux of F is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C2F⋅n2ds,

where C2 is the line segment AB― traversed from A to B, and n2 is the unit normal to C2, as shown below.

Notice that both n1 and n2 are 90∘ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of F across C2, we will use the formula

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx.

To apply the formula,

  • the curve should be parametrized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n2 must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector T(t).

We have the parametrization r(t)=(−1)i+(2t−1)j,t∈[0,1].

Therefore, P(x,y)=1−2x=1−2(−1)=3,Q(x,y)=2y=2(2t−1)=4t−2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(−1)=0,dydt=ddt(2t−1)=2.

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(3)⋅(2)−(4t−2)⋅(0)dt=∫016dt=6⋅[t]01=6⋅(1−0)=6⋅1=6

Finally, we conclude that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=6.
